title: Before the Fill: Prescription Validity, Monitoring Program Duties and Massachusetts Opioid Limits
topic: Prescription validity / Deciding whether a controlled-substance prescription may be filled
subtopic: The corresponding responsibility in 21 CFR 1306.04(a); the four determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2) and the monitoring program registration duty in 247 CMR 9.15(1); the pharmacy reporting requirement in 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) and (A)(2); the Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and DEA registration held by a prescriber of Schedules II through V or of Schedule VI only; the adult and minor opiate limits in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D with their exception and exclusion; and the outpatient pharmacist's standard under the voluntary non-opiate directive in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B
learning_objectives: State what 21 CFR 1306.04(a) places on the prescribing practitioner and on the pharmacist who fills, and identify what the word knowingly in its last sentence attaches to.
List the four determinations 247 CMR 9.15(2) requires before a pharmacist may fill a prescription, and explain why a doubt the pharmacist cannot resolve means the prescription is not filled.

Separate the pharmacist's registration and login duty under 247 CMR 9.15(1) from the pharmacy's reporting requirement under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1), and state what the reporting requirement reaches and what 700.012(A)(2) excludes.

State which registrations the Department's registration page requires of a Massachusetts prescriber of Schedules II through V and of a prescriber whose activity is limited to Schedule VI, and explain how a known registration gap bears on the decision to fill.
Apply the adult and minor limits in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(a), the exception in s. 19D(b) with its documentation, and the exclusion in s. 19D(c).
Explain what a pharmacist does, and what section 19D gives the pharmacist no authority to do, when an opiate prescription appears to exceed the prescriber's seven-day limit.

Apply the knowledge standard M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c) sets for a pharmacist in an outpatient setting, and contrast it with the reckless-or-negligent standard s. 18B(e) sets for licensed health care providers.
Say which of these provisions are federal and which are Massachusetts law, and recognise where both apply to the same fill.

orientation.text: The federal starting point is 21 CFR 1306.04(a). A prescription for a controlled substance, to be effective, must be issued for a legitimate medical purpose by an individual practitioner acting in the usual course of his professional practice. The regulation places the responsibility for the proper prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances upon the prescribing practitioner, and then adds that a corresponding responsibility rests with the pharmacist who fills the prescription. Its last sentence states what is at stake. An order purporting to be a prescription, issued not in the usual course of professional treatment or in legitimate and authorized research, is not a prescription within the meaning and intent of section 309 of the Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. 829, and the person knowingly filling such a purported prescription, as well as the person issuing it, is subject to the penalties provided for violations of the law relating to controlled substances.

Read closely, the sentence gives the pharmacist a responsibility of the pharmacist's own, resting with the pharmacist alongside the prescriber's. The question it asks is about purpose and the usual course of professional practice, so the prescriber's signature, the prescriber's registration or a prescription that is complete on its face does not by itself answer it. The penalty sentence is narrower than the responsibility: it reaches the person knowingly filling a purported prescription, which is not the same as making the pharmacist answerable for every invalid prescription that reaches the counter. What the regulation does not do is prescribe a method. 21 CFR 1306.04(a) sets out no list of warning signs, requires no call to the prescriber and prescribes no record of the pharmacist's reasoning. The course that follows from its terms is to resolve a doubt about purpose before filling rather than afterwards, because the penalties attach to knowingly filling a purported prescription, and a doubt left standing at the moment of filling is where that risk is run.

Massachusetts states the same inquiry as an express bar. Under 247 CMR 9.15(2) a pharmacist may not fill a prescription unless the pharmacist, in the exercise of his or her professional judgment, determines four things: that the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose by a practitioner acting in the usual course of his or her professional practice; that there is a valid patient-practitioner relationship; that the prescription is authentic; and that the dispensing is in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a). The structure decides cases. The default is that the prescription is not filled, and each determination is the pharmacist's to make before it is, so a doubt the pharmacist cannot resolve is a reason not to fill rather than a matter to look into after the patient has gone, and a prescriber's assurance is information for the pharmacist's judgment rather than a substitute for it. The four are separate: an authentic prescription can lack a valid patient-practitioner relationship, and a genuine relationship does not make an altered prescription authentic. The statute named in the fourth determination, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a), provides that a prescription for a controlled substance to be valid shall be issued for a legitimate medical purpose by a practitioner acting in the usual course of his professional practice, that the responsibility for the proper prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances shall be upon the prescribing practitioner, and that a corresponding responsibility shall rest with the pharmacist who fills the prescription. For a federally controlled substance dispensed in Massachusetts the federal and the Massachusetts provisions both apply to the same fill. Whether a prescription has the form and content the law requires, the follow-up owed on an oral prescription, and the rules for refills and transfers are separate subjects that this section does not teach.

Section 9.15 is headed Verifying a Practitioner's Prescriptive Authority, and two obligations that sit beside its list are not on it. The first is the monitoring program. Under 247 CMR 9.15(1) a pharmacist who dispenses medications reported to the Massachusetts Prescription Monitoring Program shall register with, and maintain login information for, the electronic system to monitor the prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances authorized by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A, known as PMP or MassPAT. The trigger is dispensing medications reported to the program, not dispensing a particular schedule, and the duty is personal: the regulation addresses the pharmacist, so a pharmacy account administered by someone else does not register the pharmacist, and registering without maintaining the login information meets only half of the duty. It is a duty of access, not a fifth determination, and nothing in 247 CMR 9.15 makes a query of the program one of the things the pharmacist must determine before filling. The second is the prescriber's registration. Despite the heading, confirming that the prescriber holds a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration is not among the four determinations either; what the registrations are, and why a known gap still matters, is taken up below.

Reporting to the program is a separate duty, and it belongs to the pharmacy. Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) the reporting requirement applies to every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses, pursuant to a prescription, a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or one the Department has classified as an additional drug, and to any pharmacy in another state, commonwealth, district or territory that delivers such a controlled substance to a person in Massachusetts. Such a pharmacy transmits to the Department or its agent the pharmacy identifier, the customer identification number and associated information as specified in the PMP Dispensing Guide issued by the Commissioner. The program's Data Submission Guide for Dispensers describes the requirement as applying to all pharmacies registered with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, to pharmacies in health facilities registered with the Department, and to out-of-state pharmacies, including mail-order pharmacies, that deliver such prescriptions to a person in Massachusetts, and it names gabapentin, which it describes as a Massachusetts Schedule VI substance, alongside federally controlled substances in Schedules II through V. Reporting status does not make gabapentin federally scheduled, and it does not mean that every Schedule VI drug is reported. Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(2) the regulation does not apply to dispensing pursuant to a medication order of a controlled substance to an inpatient in a hospital. Which drug sits in which schedule, how the Department designates an additional drug, the customer identifier required at dispensing and the deadline for each transmission are subjects of their own.

Prescribing controlled substances in Massachusetts calls for a state registration and, for federally scheduled drugs, a federal one as well. The Department of Public Health's controlled substances registration page states that Massachusetts law and Department regulations require every person who manufactures, distributes, prescribes, administers, dispenses or possesses controlled substances in Schedules II through V to be registered with both the Department, through a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration, and the federal Drug Enforcement Administration. It adds that Massachusetts law recognizes prescription drugs that are not federally scheduled, Schedule VI, as controlled substances; that practitioners who plan to manufacture, distribute, dispense, prescribe, administer or possess only Schedule VI drugs need the Massachusetts registration and not a DEA number; that both registrations are needed to conduct approved activities with controlled substances in Schedules II through V; and that the DEA and Massachusetts registrations must be for the same schedules. Two errors follow from missing that structure: treating a Schedule VI prescription as defective because its prescriber has no DEA number, and treating a DEA number as enough for a Schedule II through V prescription. For the pharmacist, confirming these registrations is not one of the determinations 247 CMR 9.15(2) enumerates, and no provision taught here tells the pharmacist to check them before every fill. A known gap is different. Which determination it defeats is not spelled out and is arguable, but a pharmacist who knows that a prescriber lacks the registration the schedule requires has an unresolved doubt about whether the prescription was issued by a practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice, and the course that is safe on any reading is not to fill until the doubt is resolved. Prescriptions from practitioners outside Massachusetts, the life of a Schedule VI prescription and the pharmacy's own controlled-substance registration are each governed by rules of their own.

Massachusetts also limits the supply on certain opiate prescriptions, and the limit is written for the prescriber. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(a), when issuing a prescription for an opiate to an adult patient for outpatient use for the first time, a practitioner shall not issue a prescription for more than a 7-day supply; and a practitioner shall not issue an opiate prescription to a minor for more than a 7-day supply at any time, and shall discuss with the minor's parent or guardian the risks associated with opiate use and the reasons why the prescription is necessary. The two sentences have different triggers. The adult limit needs an adult, outpatient use and a first-time prescription together; the minor limit carries neither the first-time condition nor the outpatient condition. Subsection (b) supplies the exception: notwithstanding subsection (a), if in the practitioner's professional medical judgment more than a 7-day supply is required to treat the adult or minor patient's acute medical condition, or is necessary for the treatment of chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or palliative care, the practitioner may issue a prescription for the quantity needed. The exception carries a record with it: the condition triggering the larger supply shall be documented in the patient's medical record, and the practitioner shall indicate that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate to address the medical condition. Subsection (c) then takes a class of medication out of the section entirely: notwithstanding subsections (a) and (b), the section does not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence. The statute names no schedule; its trigger is a prescription for an opiate.

Section 19D addresses the practitioner and says nothing to the pharmacist. It limits what a practitioner shall issue, lets the practitioner go beyond the limit on the practitioner's own professional medical judgment, and puts the supporting record in the patient's medical record rather than on the prescription. Three consequences follow at the counter. A prescription for more than a 7-day supply is not shown to be invalid by its quantity alone, because the exception can apply without anything on the prescription saying so. The section gives the pharmacist no authority to shorten the supply or to make the practitioner's documentation. And the pharmacist's own determinations under 247 CMR 9.15(2), with the corresponding responsibility under 21 CFR 1306.04(a) for a federally controlled opiate, apply to that prescription as to any other. Whether an apparently first outpatient opiate prescription for an adult, written for more than seven days with nothing to suggest the exception, obliges the pharmacist to inquire is not answered by the statute and is arguable. The course that is safe on either reading is to confirm with the prescriber, before filling, that the quantity reflects the prescriber's judgment under subsection (b). Whether a patient may ask for less than the prescribed quantity is a partial-fill question, taught with Schedule II partial fills and the thirty-day ceiling on a Schedule II prescription.

The voluntary non-opiate directive sets a limit from the patient's side. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(a) the Department establishes a voluntary non-opiate directive form, posted on its searchable website, which indicates to all practitioners that the individual shall not be administered or offered a prescription or medication order for an opiate. The individual may execute and file the form with a practitioner registered under section 7 or another authority the secretary authorizes to accept it, and may revoke it for any reason, by written or oral means. The section then measures different people by different standards. Under subsection (c) a written prescription presented at an outpatient pharmacy, or a prescription electronically transmitted to one, is presumed valid for the purposes of the section, and a pharmacist in an outpatient setting shall not be held in violation of the section for dispensing a controlled substance in contradiction to a directive, except upon evidence that the pharmacist acted knowingly against it. Under subsection (e) any board of professional licensure may limit, condition or suspend the licence of, or assess fines against, a licensed health care provider who recklessly or negligently fails to comply with a person's directive. Read together, subsection (c) states the outpatient pharmacist's standard and subsection (e) the standard for licensed health care providers generally. The outpatient pharmacist is measured by knowledge: a pharmacist who did not know of the directive is not shown to have acted knowingly merely because a more careful search would have found it, while evidence that the pharmacist knew of it and dispensed against it takes the pharmacist outside the protection. The presumption is stated for the purposes of section 18B, so it does not stand in for the determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2).

worked_examples.scenario: An electronic prescription for a Schedule II opioid arrives at a Massachusetts community pharmacy. Its electronic signature authenticated, and the prescriber holds a current Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and DEA registration for Schedules II through V. At pick-up the patient mentions that he has never met or spoken with the prescriber and that a friend arranged the prescription for him. A technician points out that the prescription is authentic and the prescriber fully registered, and says there is nothing left to decide.
steps: Separate the determinations 247 CMR 9.15(2) lists. Authenticity is 9.15(2)(c) and is satisfied on these facts; a valid patient-practitioner relationship is 9.15(2)(b), and a legitimate medical purpose by a practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice is 9.15(2)(a). Making one does not make the others.

Place the registrations. They bear on whether this prescriber may issue a Schedule II prescription at all; they do not show that this prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice, and checking them is not an enumerated determination.

Apply the federal sentence. Under 21 CFR 1306.04(a) a corresponding responsibility rests with the pharmacist who fills the prescription, and the person knowingly filling an order issued outside the usual course of professional treatment is subject to the penalties the law provides.

Apply the Massachusetts bar. 247 CMR 9.15(2) says the pharmacist may not fill unless the pharmacist makes each determination, so the patient's statement is a doubt to resolve before filling, for example with the prescriber, and not afterwards.

Decide on what the inquiry produces. If it lets the pharmacist make all four determinations, 247 CMR 9.15(2) no longer stands in the way of filling; if it does not, the regulation does not allow the prescription to be filled. Neither text prescribes a form of record, so a note of how the doubt was resolved is sound practice rather than a stated requirement.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist may not fill on the strength of authentication and registration alone and has to be able to determine a valid patient-practitioner relationship and a legitimate medical purpose before filling. The error the scenario invites is the technician's: treating an authentic prescription from a registered prescriber as a valid one, when authenticity is only one of four determinations and registration is not among them.

worked_examples.scenario: Two prescriptions reach a Massachusetts pharmacy on the same morning. The first, for a Schedule VI antibiotic, comes from a Massachusetts practitioner whose Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration covers Schedule VI only and who has no DEA registration. The second, for a Schedule IV benzodiazepine, comes from a Massachusetts practitioner who holds a DEA registration for Schedules II through V, and the pharmacist knows from a call to the office earlier that week that this practitioner's Massachusetts registration covers Schedule VI only. A colleague says the first prescription is invalid because every prescriber needs a DEA number and the second is fine because the DEA number is there.
steps: Start with the Department's registration page: practitioners who plan to manufacture, distribute, dispense, prescribe, administer or possess only Schedule VI drugs need a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and not a DEA number. The first prescriber's lack of a DEA registration is not a defect in a Schedule VI prescription.

For Schedules II through V the page requires both registrations, and requires the DEA and Massachusetts registrations to be for the same schedules. A DEA registration covering Schedule IV does not supply the Massachusetts registration the second prescriber lacks for that schedule.

Turn to the pharmacist's own rules. Confirming registrations is not one of the four determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2), so the regulation does not direct the pharmacist to check every prescriber's registrations before every fill.

Here, though, the pharmacist knows of the gap. Which determination it defeats is not spelled out and is arguable; the course that is safe on any reading is to treat it as an unresolved doubt about whether the prescription was issued by a practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice, and not to fill the Schedule IV prescription until it is resolved.
worked_examples.resolution: The Schedule VI prescription is not defective for want of a DEA number, and the Schedule IV prescription should not be filled while the pharmacist knows the prescriber lacks the Massachusetts registration for that schedule. The error the scenario invites is the colleague's pair of mistakes: treating a DEA number as required for every prescription, and treating it as sufficient for a Schedule II through V prescription.

worked_examples.scenario: Three prescriptions reach a Massachusetts outpatient pharmacy. An adult who, on the pharmacy's records and her own account, has never been prescribed an opiate presents a prescription for a 10-day supply of an opiate after dental surgery, with nothing on it about why more than seven days is needed. A 15-year-old who has filled opiate prescriptions before presents one for a 10-day supply. An adult presents a prescription for a 30-day supply of buprenorphine-naloxone for opioid dependence. A technician proposes cutting the first two to seven days and holding the third for the same reason.
steps: Identify the actor. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(a) says a practitioner shall not issue more than a 7-day supply; it is a limit on issuing, and the section addresses nothing to the pharmacist. The discussion with a minor's parent or guardian is the practitioner's duty as well.

Test each trigger. The first prescription meets all three adult conditions: an adult, outpatient use and a first opiate prescription. The second meets the minor sentence, which applies at any time, so the minor's earlier opiate prescriptions do not take it outside the limit.

Look for the exception before concluding anything. Under s. 19D(b) the practitioner may issue the quantity needed where, in the practitioner's professional medical judgment, more than seven days is required for an acute medical condition, or for chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or palliative care, with the triggering condition documented in the patient's medical record and an indication that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate. That record is not required on the prescription, so its absence from the prescription proves nothing.

Apply subsection (c) to the third prescription. The section does not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence, so the seven-day limit is no reason to hold buprenorphine-naloxone prescribed for opioid dependence.

Decide what the pharmacist does with the first two. The statute gives the pharmacist no authority to cut the supply, and the quantity alone does not show that either prescription is invalid; but the determinations under 247 CMR 9.15(2) still have to be made. Whether the pharmacist must inquire is arguable, and the course that is safe on either reading is to confirm with each prescriber, before filling, that the quantity reflects the prescriber's judgment under subsection (b).
worked_examples.resolution: The third prescription is outside section 19D altogether, and section 19D supplies no authority for the pharmacist to rewrite the first two to seven days; the safe course is to confirm the exception with each prescriber before filling. The error the scenario invites is treating the prescriber's limit as a ceiling the pharmacist enforces by editing the quantity, with two further errors behind it: copying the adult first-time condition into the minor rule, and overlooking the exclusion for medications designed for the treatment of opioid dependence.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient filed a voluntary non-opiate directive with her primary care practitioner. Months later a practitioner in another practice electronically transmits a prescription for an opiate to her usual outpatient pharmacy, and the first pharmacist on duty dispenses it without knowing of the directive; nothing in the pharmacy's records mentioned it. The next week the patient tells a second pharmacist at the counter that she has a directive on file and does not want opiates, and the second pharmacist, knowing that, dispenses another electronically transmitted opiate prescription from the same practitioner. A manager says both pharmacists are equally exposed because each should have checked.
steps: Start with the presumption. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c) a prescription electronically transmitted to an outpatient pharmacy is presumed valid for the purposes of the section.

Apply the outpatient pharmacist's standard to the first pharmacist. A pharmacist in an outpatient setting shall not be held in violation of the section for dispensing a controlled substance in contradiction to a directive, except upon evidence that the pharmacist acted knowingly against it. The first pharmacist did not know, so whether a closer search would have found the directive is not the question the subsection asks.

Apply the same test to the second pharmacist. The patient told her of the directive and she dispensed knowing of it; that is evidence of acting knowingly against the directive, and it takes her outside the protection subsection (c) gives.

Place the manager's standard where the statute puts it. Subsection (e) lets a board of professional licensure act against a licensed health care provider who recklessly or negligently fails to comply with a directive; read together with subsection (c), that is the standard for providers generally, while the outpatient pharmacist is measured by knowledge.
Keep the presumption in its place. It is stated for the purposes of section 18B, so it does not relieve either pharmacist of the determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2).
worked_examples.resolution: The first pharmacist is within the protection of subsection (c), and the second, who acted knowingly against the directive, is not. The error the scenario invites is the manager's: applying a should-have-checked, negligence-style standard to the outpatient pharmacist, when the section measures that pharmacist by knowledge and states the reckless-or-negligent standard for licensed health care providers generally.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist starts work at a Massachusetts community pharmacy that dispenses Schedule II through V controlled substances and gabapentin. The pharmacy's dispensing data are uploaded each day through an account the pharmacy manager holds, and the manager tells her that the upload covers everyone, so she has no need to register with the monitoring program. On her first day she also asks whether gabapentin really has to be reported, since it is not federally scheduled, and whether 247 CMR 9.15 requires her to check the program before every controlled-substance fill.
steps: Separate the two duties by actor. 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) places the reporting requirement on the pharmacy, which transmits the pharmacy identifier, customer identification number and associated information specified in the PMP Dispensing Guide; the manager's upload serves that pharmacy duty.

247 CMR 9.15(1) places a different duty on the pharmacist: a pharmacist who dispenses medications reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program shall register with, and maintain login information for, the system known as PMP or MassPAT. She dispenses such medications, so the duty is hers, and the pharmacy's upload account does not discharge it.

Answer the gabapentin question from the reporting texts. 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) reaches additional drugs the Department has classified as well as Schedules II through V, and the dispenser guide names gabapentin, describing it as a Massachusetts Schedule VI substance; reporting it does not make it federally scheduled.

Answer the last question from what 247 CMR 9.15 says. The registration duty is a duty of access, and the four determinations in 9.15(2) do not include a query of the program, so 247 CMR 9.15 does not itself make a check before every fill a requirement; the determinations themselves still have to be made on each prescription.
worked_examples.resolution: She has to register with the program and maintain her login information, the pharmacy reports its gabapentin dispensing along with its Schedule II through V dispensing, and 247 CMR 9.15 does not itself require a query before each fill. The error the scenario invites is the manager's conflation of the pharmacy's reporting account with the pharmacist's personal registration duty.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 CFR 1306.04(a), upon whom does the responsibility for the proper prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances rest, and what rests with the pharmacist?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The responsibility is upon the prescribing practitioner; a corresponding responsibility rests with the pharmacist who fills the prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: under 21 CFR 1306.04(a) a pharmacist is subject to the penalties for filling any order that later proves not to be a valid prescription.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The penalties attach to the person knowingly filling a purported prescription issued not in the usual course of professional treatment or in legitimate and authorized research, as well as to the person issuing it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the four determinations 247 CMR 9.15(2) requires before a pharmacist may fill a prescription.
retrieval_prompts.answer: That the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose by a practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice; that there is a valid patient-practitioner relationship; that the prescription is authentic; and that the dispensing is in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: confirming the prescriber's Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration is one of the determinations listed in 247 CMR 9.15(2).
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The section is headed Verifying a Practitioner's Prescriptive Authority, but registration is not among the four enumerated determinations.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: 247 CMR 9.15(2) is satisfied once the pharmacist confirms that the prescription is authentic.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Authenticity is one of four determinations. The pharmacist must also determine that the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose by a practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice, that there is a valid patient-practitioner relationship, and that the dispensing is in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 9.15(1) require, and of whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacist who dispenses medications reported to the Massachusetts Prescription Monitoring Program shall register with, and maintain login information for, the system authorized by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A, known as PMP or MassPAT.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy's daily data upload runs through the manager's account. Does that satisfy a staff pharmacist's duty under 247 CMR 9.15(1)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. The regulation places the registration and login duty on the pharmacist who dispenses reported medications; the pharmacy's upload serves the pharmacy's separate reporting requirement under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which dispensing does 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) require a pharmacy to report, and what does 700.012(A)(2) exclude?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Dispensing, pursuant to a prescription, of a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or one the Department has classified as an additional drug, including delivery of such a substance by an out-of-state pharmacy to a person in Massachusetts. Dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital is excluded.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: because a pharmacy reports its gabapentin dispensing to the Massachusetts program, gabapentin is federally scheduled.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The dispenser guide names gabapentin as reportable and describes it as a Massachusetts Schedule VI substance; reporting status does not make it federally scheduled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Massachusetts practitioner will prescribe only Schedule VI drugs. Which registration does the Department's registration page say the practitioner needs?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration, and not a DEA number.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: For Schedules II through V, what does the Department's registration page require about the two registrations beyond holding both?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That the DEA and Massachusetts registrations be for the same schedules.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(a), which three facts together trigger the adult 7-day limit, and how does the minor limit differ?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An adult patient, outpatient use and a first-time opiate prescription. The minor limit applies to an opiate prescription at any time, without the first-time or outpatient conditions, and the practitioner must also discuss the risks of opiate use and the reasons for the prescription with the parent or guardian.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the four situations in which s. 19D(b) lets a practitioner prescribe more than a 7-day supply, and the two things the statute requires when the practitioner does.
retrieval_prompts.answer: An acute medical condition, chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis, and palliative care. The condition triggering the larger supply is documented in the patient's medical record, and the practitioner indicates that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate to address the medical condition.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D apply to buprenorphine-naloxone prescribed for opioid dependence?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Subsection (c) provides that the section does not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: An adult's first outpatient opiate prescription is written for 10 days with nothing on it about an exception. What does s. 19D itself direct the pharmacist to do?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Nothing; the section is addressed to the practitioner, and the exception's record belongs in the patient's medical record rather than on the prescription. The pharmacist's determinations under 247 CMR 9.15(2) still apply, and confirming the prescriber's judgment under s. 19D(b) before filling is the safe course.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c), an outpatient pharmacist who dispenses against a directive she did not know about, but could have found with more care, is in violation of the section.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. A pharmacist in an outpatient setting shall not be held in violation for dispensing in contradiction to a directive except upon evidence that the pharmacist acted knowingly against it; carelessness is not that standard.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under s. 18B, how may an individual revoke a voluntary non-opiate directive, and what standard does subsection (e) apply to licensed health care providers?
retrieval_prompts.answer: For any reason, by written or oral means. Under subsection (e) a board of professional licensure may limit, condition or suspend the licence of, or fine, a licensed health care provider who recklessly or negligently fails to comply with the directive.

quick_review.text: Under 21 CFR 1306.04(a) a prescription for a controlled substance, to be effective, must be issued for a legitimate medical purpose by an individual practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice; the responsibility is upon the prescribing practitioner, and a corresponding responsibility rests with the pharmacist who fills.

The person knowingly filling a purported prescription issued outside the usual course of professional treatment or legitimate and authorized research, as well as the person issuing it, is subject to the penalties for controlled-substance violations.

Under 247 CMR 9.15(2) a pharmacist may not fill a prescription unless the pharmacist determines a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice, a valid patient-practitioner relationship, authenticity, and dispensing in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a).

The four determinations are separate and are the pharmacist's own: authenticity does not establish the relationship, and a prescriber's assurance does not replace the pharmacist's professional judgment.

Under 247 CMR 9.15(1) a pharmacist who dispenses medications reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program registers with, and maintains login information for, PMP or MassPAT; a pharmacy account does not discharge that personal duty.
Neither registration with the program nor a query of it is one of the determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2).

Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) a pharmacy reports dispensing, pursuant to a prescription, of Schedule II through V controlled substances and additional drugs, and an out-of-state pharmacy delivering such a substance to a person in Massachusetts reports as well; 700.012(A)(2) excludes dispensing pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient.

The dispenser guide names gabapentin, which it describes as a Massachusetts Schedule VI substance, as reportable; reporting does not make gabapentin federally scheduled, and not every Schedule VI drug is reported.

For Schedules II through V a Massachusetts prescriber needs both a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and a DEA registration, for the same schedules; for activity limited to Schedule VI the Massachusetts registration is needed and a DEA number is not.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(a) bars a practitioner from issuing more than a 7-day supply on an adult's first opiate prescription for outpatient use, and on an opiate prescription to a minor at any time, subject to subsections (b) and (c), and requires a discussion of risks and reasons with the minor's parent or guardian.

Section 19D(b) permits the quantity needed for an acute medical condition, chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or palliative care, with the triggering condition documented in the medical record and an indication that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate; s. 19D(c) excludes medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.

Section 19D is addressed to the practitioner: quantity alone does not show a prescription invalid, the statute gives the pharmacist no authority to shorten it, and the pharmacist's own determinations still apply.

Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c) a pharmacist in an outpatient setting is not held in violation for dispensing against a directive except upon evidence of knowing action; under s. 18B(e) a board may act against a licensed health care provider who recklessly or negligently fails to comply.

A voluntary non-opiate directive may be executed and filed with a practitioner registered under section 7 or another authority the secretary authorizes, and may be revoked for any reason by written or oral means.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription for a controlled substance is presented for filling in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Make the four determinations of 247 CMR 9.15(2) before filling, and for a federally controlled substance keep in view the corresponding responsibility 21 CFR 1306.04(a) places on the pharmacist who fills. If a determination cannot be made, do not fill.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is authentic and the prescriber's registrations are current, but facts raise a doubt about its purpose or about the patient-practitioner relationship.
decision_logic.action: Treat the doubt as unresolved until it is resolved, for example with the prescriber; authenticity and registration do not answer it, and filling first with a plan to look into it later is what 247 CMR 9.15(2) rules out.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist dispenses medications reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program.
decision_logic.action: Register personally with PMP or MassPAT and maintain the login information, without relying on the pharmacy's reporting account.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy dispenses a Schedule II through V controlled substance or an additional drug such as gabapentin.
decision_logic.action: Treat dispensing pursuant to a prescription as one the pharmacy reports under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1); dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital is outside the regulation under 700.012(A)(2).

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription comes from a Massachusetts practitioner who has no DEA registration.
decision_logic.action: Do not treat the missing DEA number as a defect; activity limited to Schedule VI needs the Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and not a DEA number.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist knows that a Massachusetts prescriber of a Schedule II through V drug lacks the DEA or the Massachusetts registration for that schedule.
decision_logic.action: Treat the gap as an unresolved doubt bearing on the determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2), and do not fill until it is resolved.

decision_logic.condition: An opiate prescription for more than a 7-day supply is presented.
decision_logic.action: Ask first whether the medication is designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence, which s. 19D does not reach; then whether the patient is an adult with a first opiate prescription for outpatient use, or a minor. If the limit applies and nothing indicates the s. 19D(b) exception, confirm with the prescriber before filling rather than rewriting the quantity.

decision_logic.condition: An outpatient pharmacist has dispensed a controlled substance to a patient who had filed a voluntary non-opiate directive.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether there is evidence that the pharmacist acted knowingly against the directive. Without it, s. 18B(c) says the pharmacist shall not be held in violation of the section; recklessness or negligence is the subsection (e) standard for licensed health care providers generally.

decision_logic.condition: An outpatient pharmacist knows that the patient has a directive and receives an opiate prescription for her.
decision_logic.action: Recognise that dispensing with knowledge of the directive is the conduct s. 18B(c) excepts from its protection, and that the presumption of validity does not change that; the course that keeps the pharmacist within the protection is not to dispense against the directive.

ma_vs_federal.text: Federally, 21 CFR 1306.04(a) places a corresponding responsibility on the pharmacist who fills a prescription for a controlled substance; in Massachusetts, 247 CMR 9.15(2)(d) requires the pharmacist to determine that the dispensing is in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a). A fill of a federally controlled substance in Massachusetts answers to both.

Massachusetts adds an express rule the federal sentence does not state: under 247 CMR 9.15(2) the pharmacist may not fill unless the pharmacist determines a legitimate medical purpose, a valid patient-practitioner relationship, authenticity and accordance with s. 19(a).

A Massachusetts prescriber of Schedules II through V needs a federal DEA registration and a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration for the same schedules; Schedule VI is a Massachusetts category of controlled substance, and activity limited to it needs the Massachusetts registration without a DEA number.

Reporting to the Massachusetts program follows the Massachusetts reporting texts: the dispenser guide lists gabapentin, which it describes as a Massachusetts Schedule VI substance, apart from the federally controlled substances in Schedules II through V, and reporting does not change a drug's federal status.

The seven-day opiate limit and the voluntary non-opiate directive are Massachusetts provisions; the federal provision taught here, 21 CFR 1306.04(a), states no supply limit and says nothing about a directive.

exceptions.text: Section 19D(b) lets the practitioner issue the quantity needed beyond a 7-day supply for an adult's or a minor's acute medical condition, chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or palliative care, with the triggering condition documented in the patient's medical record and an indication that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate.
Section 19D(c) provides that the section, limit and exception alike, does not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.
The protection in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c) gives way upon evidence that the outpatient pharmacist acted knowingly against the directive.
105 CMR 700.012(A)(2) takes dispensing pursuant to a medication order of a controlled substance to an inpatient in a hospital outside the reporting regulation.
A practitioner whose activity is limited to Schedule VI needs the Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and not a DEA number.
247 CMR 9.15(2) states no exception to the requirement that all four determinations be made before a prescription is filled.

timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacist may not fill unless the four determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2) have been made; a doubt left to be investigated after filling does not satisfy the regulation.

timing_deadlines.event: An adult patient's first opiate prescription for outpatient use
timing_deadlines.consequence: The practitioner may exceed it under s. 19D(b), with the triggering condition documented in the patient's medical record and an indication that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate; under s. 19D(c) the limit does not reach medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.

timing_deadlines.event: An opiate prescription for a minor
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than a 7-day supply, at any time
timing_deadlines.consequence: The limit applies whether or not the minor has had opiate prescriptions before, subject to s. 19D(b) and to the exclusion in s. 19D(c), and the practitioner discusses the risks of opiate use and the reasons for the prescription with the parent or guardian.

forms_records.text: The electronic system to monitor the prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances authorized by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A is known as PMP or MassPAT; 247 CMR 9.15(1) requires the dispensing pharmacist's own registration with it and maintained login information for it.

A pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012 transmits to the Department or its agent the pharmacy identifier, customer identification number and associated information as specified in the PMP Dispensing Guide issued by the Commissioner.

The program's Data Submission Guide for Dispensers states that pharmacies are required to submit dispensing information on federally controlled substances in Schedules II through V and on gabapentin, and that the requirements apply to pharmacies registered with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, to pharmacies in health facilities registered with the Department, and to out-of-state pharmacies, including mail-order pharmacies, delivering such prescriptions to a person in Massachusetts.

The prescriber's credentials are a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration issued by the Department of Public Health and, for Schedules II through V, a DEA registration; the two must be for the same schedules.

Where a practitioner prescribes more than a 7-day supply under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(b), the triggering condition is documented in the patient's medical record and the practitioner indicates that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate; the statute places neither record on the prescription and neither task on the pharmacist.

The voluntary non-opiate directive form is established by the Department and posted on its searchable website; the individual executes and files it with a practitioner registered under section 7 or another authority the secretary authorizes to accept it, and may revoke it for any reason by written or oral means.

Neither 247 CMR 9.15(2) nor 21 CFR 1306.04(a) prescribes a form for recording how the pharmacist reached the determinations or resolved a doubt; a note of the resolution is sound practice rather than a stated requirement of either text.

role_duties.duty: Bears the responsibility for the proper prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances, and issues a controlled-substance prescription for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice under 21 CFR 1306.04(a).

role_duties.role: Pharmacist who fills a controlled-substance prescription, under federal law
role_duties.duty: Carries the corresponding responsibility under 21 CFR 1306.04(a), and is subject to the penalties for controlled-substance violations if knowingly filling a purported prescription.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist filling a prescription in Massachusetts
role_duties.duty: Does not fill unless, in the pharmacist's own professional judgment, the four determinations of 247 CMR 9.15(2) have been made, including that the dispensing accords with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a).

role_duties.role: Pharmacist who dispenses medications reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program
role_duties.duty: Registers personally with PMP or MassPAT and maintains login information for it under 247 CMR 9.15(1).

Transmits the pharmacy identifier, customer identification number and associated information specified in the PMP Dispensing Guide for each reportable dispensing, pursuant to a prescription, of a Schedule II through V controlled substance or an additional drug.
Falls within the reporting requirement of 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) when it delivers a Schedule II through V controlled substance or an additional drug to a person in Massachusetts.
Establishes the voluntary non-opiate directive form and posts it on its searchable website.

role_duties.role: Practitioner conducting activity with Schedule II through V controlled substances
role_duties.duty: Holds both a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration and a DEA registration, and holds them for the same schedules.

role_duties.role: Practitioner whose activity is limited to Schedule VI
role_duties.duty: Holds a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration; a DEA number is not required for that activity.

Does not issue more than a 7-day supply on an adult's first opiate prescription for outpatient use or on an opiate prescription to a minor unless s. 19D(b) applies or the medication is one s. 19D(c) excludes, discusses the risks and the reasons with a minor's parent or guardian, and, in issuing a larger supply under s. 19D(b), indicates that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate, with the triggering condition documented in the patient's medical record.

role_duties.role: Individual who does not want opiates
role_duties.duty: May execute and file a voluntary non-opiate directive with a practitioner registered under section 7 or another authority the secretary authorizes, and may revoke it for any reason by written or oral means.
Stays within the protection of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18B(c) unless there is evidence that the pharmacist acted knowingly against the patient's directive.
May limit, condition or suspend the licence of, or assess fines against, a licensed health care provider who recklessly or negligently fails to comply with a person's directive.

common_traps.text: Treating a prescriber's DEA registration, or an authenticated electronic signature, as the answer to whether a prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice.

Reading the word knowingly in 21 CFR 1306.04(a) as a condition of the corresponding responsibility itself; the responsibility rests with the pharmacist who fills, and knowledge is what the penalty sentence attaches to filling a purported prescription.
Filling first and investigating later. 247 CMR 9.15(2) says the pharmacist may not fill unless the determinations have been made.
Adding a registration check or a monitoring-program query to the determinations in 247 CMR 9.15(2) because of the section heading or the registration duty beside it.
Assuming the pharmacy's reporting account satisfies the pharmacist's own duty to register with the program and maintain login information.
Treating gabapentin's reporting status as a change of schedule, or assuming that every Schedule VI drug is reported.
Treating a DEA number as required for every prescription, or as sufficient for a Schedule II through V prescription without the Massachusetts registration for the same schedule.
Carrying the adult's first-time and outpatient conditions into the minor limit, which applies to an opiate prescription at any time.

Treating the seven-day limit as a ceiling the pharmacist enforces by rewriting the quantity, or as proof that a longer prescription is invalid; the statute addresses the practitioner and rests the exception on the practitioner's judgment, with the triggering condition documented in the patient's medical record.
Applying section 19D to a medication designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.
Assuming the seven-day limit turns on schedule; s. 19D names no schedule, and its trigger is a prescription for an opiate.

Applying the reckless-or-negligent standard of s. 18B(e) to the outpatient pharmacist, or treating the presumption of validity in s. 18B(c) as a general validation that displaces the pharmacist's own determinations.
Assuming a non-opiate directive can be revoked only in writing, when s. 18B(a) allows written or oral revocation for any reason.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Prescribed for opioid dependence, it is a medication designed for the treatment of opioid dependence, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(c) provides that the seven-day section does not apply to such medications.

An adult's first outpatient prescription for this opiate is limited by s. 19D(a) to a 7-day supply unless the practitioner invokes s. 19D(b); a longer prescription is one to confirm with the prescriber before filling, and s. 19D gives the pharmacist no authority to shorten it.
Section 19D names no schedule, so tramadol's placement in Schedule IV is not itself a reason to set the seven-day limit aside for an opiate prescription.

The dispenser guide names gabapentin, which it describes as a Massachusetts Schedule VI substance, as reportable; reporting does not make it federally scheduled, and a practitioner whose activity is limited to Schedule VI needs the Massachusetts registration and not a DEA number to prescribe it.
